**The package has to exist upstream before the workflow can update it.**
Nigel's Windows machine disables the MSI Restart Manager by policy, so installers must close running apps themselves

This machine sets `DisableAutomaticApplicationShutdown = 1` under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer`, so the Windows Installer Restart Manager never runs here. Installers cannot rely on Windows closing a running program before replacing its files; they fall back to a Retry/Cancel FilesInUse dialog and end in 1603, which looks like the installer crashing.

**Why:** it is a hardening/managed-baseline policy, not something Loadout set, and it is invisible unless you read an MSI verbose log — the package installs and upgrades perfectly on a machine where the Restart Manager works. It cost a release (0.3.0 could not upgrade over 0.2.0) before it was found.
To tell a blank VS Code window from a loaded one, enumerate window titles with EnumWindows; log directories and MainWindowTitle both lie

When diagnosing whether VS Code actually opened a folder, read the window titles: a loaded window is `<folder> - Visual Studio Code`, a blank one is just `Visual Studio Code`. Enumerate them with `EnumWindows` via `Add-Type`, not with `Get-Process Code | MainWindowTitle`.

**Why:** two obvious instruments are both wrong. `MainWindowTitle` reports only the main process's primary window, so with six windows open it shows one — it made a failing command look like it had worked, and I reported that before catching it. And an empty session log directory under `%APPDATA%\Code\logs\` does **not** mean a broken instance; the CLI writes one on every invocation, healthy or not. That false signal was load-bearing in four attempted fixes of the blank-window bug across 0.9.5–0.9.8 and sent every one of them at the wrong cause.

The after-edit hook is handled (ClaudeAdapter rewrites it to LauncherInvocation.Current() at launch), but the status line installer still writes Environment.ProcessPath alone, which omits loadout.dll on a development build

The after-edit hook no longer names the launcher at all: the settings file carries 'loadout docs refresh --hook --project <slug>' and ClaudeAdapter.AddSettingsAsync rewrites it to LauncherInvocation.Current() at launch, which is where the dotnet-host case is now handled. The status line installer still writes Environment.ProcessPath alone.

Loadout tests that fail only in the full suite have three causes that look identical - a disturbed binary, a real concurrency bug, and Windows refusing to start any more processes (settled: runner thread count)

Tests under `tests/Loadout.Tests/Contract/*` spawn the real `loadout.exe`, so disturbing that binary mid-run makes them fail for reasons unrelated to the code. Seen twice: killing `loadout` by name during a run, and running the suite immediately after `dotnet build` replaced the binary.

**But "fails in the full suite, passes in isolation" is also exactly what a race looks like**, and xUnit runs collections in parallel. On 27 August 2026 two `CliContractTests` failed that way twice; I twice reached for this note and twice nearly filed a genuine defect as a flake. The cause was `Program.CommandNames()` lazily populating a shared mutable `HashSet` with no synchronisation.
In this environment, inline Bash heredocs turn '\\\\' into '\\' and choke on quotes, so multi-line scripts must be written with the Write tool and run from the scratchpad

Inline `python - <<'EOF'` heredocs in the Bash tool here corrupt backslash escapes (`'\\'` arrives as `'\'`) and sometimes fail to parse at all with "unexpected EOF while looking for matching quote", even with a quoted delimiter. Twice in one session this produced a mutation that never applied and a C# edit that broke the build.
**Why:** the tool's shell layer on this Windows machine rewrites the heredoc body before Python sees it; Git Bash printf has the same trait.

Windows PowerShell 5.1 reports an empty ExitCode from Start-Process -PassThru when output is redirected, so a script on a clean Windows image compares every exit code against nothing; stage pwsh 7 rather than reworking the script

Windows PowerShell 5.1 does not expose ExitCode on a process created by Start-Process -PassThru when output is redirected: it reads as empty, while the identical call under pwsh 7 returns the code. A clean Windows image has only 5.1, so any verification script run there compares every exit code against nothing and can report a failure it cannot explain, or a pass it has not earned.

Caching the process handle before waiting, and a second no-argument WaitForExit, both fail to recover the code under 5.1. Only constructing the process directly through System.Diagnostics.ProcessStartInfo works. Staging pwsh 7 into the environment is the cheaper fix where the script is shared with CI, because it leaves the script alone and makes the local run the same run CI does.

This repository restores with --locked-mode, so a bump that misses any of the seven packages.lock.json files fails hard with NU1004; comment '@dependabot recreate' rather than hand-editing the branch, which a later rebase can discard

This repository restores with --locked-mode and manages package versions centrally, so a bump that updates Directory.Packages.props and only some of the seven packages.lock.json files is a hard failure rather than a warning: NU1004, 'Mismatch between the requestedVersion of a lock file dependency marked as CentralTransitive and the version specified in the central package management file'.

Commenting '@dependabot recreate' on the pull request regenerates the branch with every lock file, which is the cheap fix and leaves the change as Dependabot's rather than hand-edited. Pushing a correction to its branch instead risks a later rebase discarding it.

GitHub's git/ref/tags returns the tag object's SHA for an annotated tag, not the commit's, so a correctly pinned action reads as a supply-chain mismatch until you dereference through git/tags/<sha> and compare .object.sha

GitHub's git/ref/tags endpoint returns the tag object's SHA for an annotated tag, not the commit's. Comparing that against a workflow's pinned SHA shows a mismatch for a pin that is correct, and both azure/login and softprops/action-gh-release use annotated tags. Dereference through git/tags/<sha> and compare .object.sha, or the check reports a supply chain problem where there is none.
Check .object.type before believing the answer: it reads 'tag' for an annotated tag and 'commit' for a lightweight one, and only the second can be compared directly.

Minor for new capability, patch for repairs only, decided from the actual commit range; release notes go in the annotated tag's BODY because %(contents:body) drops the subject line, and confirm the tag carries the bumped Directory.Build.props before pushing
Loadout follows semver. While it is on 0.x: a release adding user-facing capability takes a **minor** bump (0.1.0 → 0.2.0); a release of repairs only takes a **patch** (0.1.0 → 0.1.1).

**Why:** nothing in the repository documents this — I checked README, docs/ and the workflows on 24 August 2026 and found no policy — so it was previously a judgement made per release. Agreed with Nigel that day, after 0.2.0 shipped with MCP management, launcher remediation and the screen frame: three new capabilities, so `0.1.1` would have understated it.

Reverting a mutation check with git checkout wiped a whole afternoon's uncommitted edits; restore from a copy of the file instead

When mutation-checking a test on uncommitted work, never undo the mutation with `git checkout -- <file>`. That restores the file to the last commit, which throws away every uncommitted edit in it, not just the mutation.

**Why:** On 8 September 2026 this discarded the whole launcher restyle in two files and they had to be re-applied edit by edit. The mutation result was still valid, but the recovery cost more than the check.
